title: Market Cap, Supply, and FDV
objectives: Why price per coin tells you nothing, and market cap tells you the size
What FDV is and what the gap between it and market cap means
Why the circulating supply figure is the least trustworthy number on the page

steps.title: The number that actually sizes a token
steps.body:
"$0.0001, that's cheap. $200, that's expensive." Almost everyone starts here, and it's the wrong number, because price per coin means nothing on its own. Ten trillion coins at a tenth of a cent is a billion-dollar asset.

The number that sizes a token is <Term id="market_cap">market cap</Term>:

`market cap = price × circulating supply`

Two tokens, same maths:

- Token A: $0.0001 per coin, 10,000,000,000,000 coins → **$1,000,000,000**.
- Token B: $200 per coin, 10,000 coins → **$2,000,000**.

Token A looks two million times cheaper per coin. It is actually 500 times larger. Simply put: unit price is a vanity metric, market cap is the size. Multiply before you judge.

steps.title: FDV, and the low-float trap
steps.body:
Most launches don't release all their tokens at once. A typical project starts with 5-10% <Term id="float">float</Term> and locks the rest for the team, the investors, and future rewards, handing them out on a schedule that runs for years.

So there are two sizes to know, not one:

- **Market cap** = price × <Term id="circulating_supply">circulating supply</Term>: what exists and can trade today.
- **<Term id="fdv">FDV</Term>** = price × <Term id="total_supply">total supply</Term>: what the whole thing would be worth if every locked token counted at today's price.

Take a project with a $50M market cap and a $1B FDV. That gap says 95% of the supply is still outside the market. Every <Term id="unlock">unlock</Term> releases new coins that someone has to buy just to keep the price flat, and the people receiving them usually paid far below market for them. That's what "low float, high FDV" means: a small-looking asset that is mostly still in the pipeline.

FDV is not automatically a red flag - plenty of serious projects lock supply on purpose. But an FDV without an unlock schedule attached is a headline, not a valuation.

steps.title: Where the circulating number comes from
steps.body:
Market cap is only as good as its supply figure, and that figure isn't read straight off the chain.

The token's total supply *is* on-chain and exact. The circulating supply is not. It's assembled from addresses the project itself reports as locked - team wallets, treasury, vesting contracts - which data providers subtract from the total. The project writes the list.

That's fine when it's honest, and slippery when it isn't. Treasury tokens can be staked or lent to market makers, which quietly blurs the line between locked and circulating. Two dashboards can disagree about the same token because they were handed different lists.

Which is why the useful habit isn't to trust a number but to check the pieces: the unlock schedule, and who holds what. A single figure on a single site is a starting point, not an answer.

questions.prompt: Token XYZ trades at $2.00, with 10 million circulating and 100 million total supply. What are its market cap and FDV?
questions.explainWrong: Market cap is price × circulating, FDV is price × total: $20M and $200M.

questions.prompt: Why is a 'low float, high FDV' token risky for someone holding it long?
options: Future unlocks release early holders' tokens, and that selling needs fresh buyers to absorb
questions.explainRight: Unlocks add supply that has to be bought to hold the price flat, and early holders usually sell.
questions.explainWrong: Locked tokens vest to teams and investors, who sell into the market over time.
